source.title: Discovering Universal Geometry in Embeddings with ICA
source.authors: Hiroaki Yamagiwa; Momose Oyama; Hidetoshi Shimodaira

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or garbling; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Measures whether independently obtained embeddings share aligned semantic axes, using ICA and cross-correlation rather than a scale sweep or the original studies’ methods.
record.gate_note: The paper reports cross-correlation/axis-alignment findings and cross-lingual retrieval results that bear on representation alignment. Its word-intrusion and downstream-task results concern interpretability or embedding utility, not convergence, so they are not rows. The paper does not test how alignment changes with model size or capability.
record.test_reason: The study applies ICA separately to independently trained embeddings and checks with cross-correlations whether the same interpretable axes recur. It compares 7 languages' fastText, fastText vs BERT, five ImageNet models, and image models vs fastText. It also measures how well a permutation map or a linear map recovers translations. These results bear on V5 (recurring interpretable features) and V4 (simple maps between models). There is no scale or capability sweep and no seed comparison.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors conclude that ICA reveals interpretable, sparse axes that are nearly universal across languages, algorithms and modalities, and that a few axes represent each word. They also claim ICA 'performed comparably to the supervised baselines' in cross-lingual alignment. That is overstated for 157langs (19.48 vs LS 84.72) and holds mainly against Proc after random distortion.
record.recipe_differences: Uses post-processing with whitening and ICA, axis matching, and cross-lingual retrieval; it is not a reproduction of the original sources’ methods. Axis matching uses translation pairs in the cross-lingual analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment depends on the transformation: ICA is described as strongly aligned across tested embeddings, while PCA is less favorable. Cross-lingual retrieval also differs between 157langs-fastText and MUSE-fastText.

fits_no_version.finding: ICA axes of five ImageNet models, including non-CLIP ResMLP-12 and Swin-S, match fastText word axes through class-name words; an example is an alcohol axis. This is cross-modal alignment shown statically, without paired captions or any capability trend.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Vision and language embeddings share interpretable independent axes even when the vision model was not trained with text (static cross-modal correspondence).

record.problems: Several central cross-correlation results are presented in figures without numerical values in the text. The cross-lingual retrieval analysis uses translation pairs for axis matching, and the paper states that its method cannot perform this matching without such pairs. No model-size or capability comparison is reported.
record.rows_left_out: Table 15 reports individual target-language retrieval accuracies for the conditions aggregated in Table 3. These per-language values were not extracted separately; Table 3 values, which the paper states are averages over five target languages, are recorded in R9–R24.

untested.parts: No model-size or capability sweep; no trend of alignment with scale.
Image-fastText link uses ImageNet class-name words, not paired captions. There is no test of alignment rising as the vision or language model improves.
No stitching, no relative representations, and no mapping without paired data. The authors state that axis matching needs translation pairs.
No neuron-level, SAE-feature or circuit comparison; only ICA axes of final or penultimate embeddings.
No variation of the similarity measure, its settings, or the input distribution. ICA vs PCA is a choice of basis within the same whitened space, not a similarity metric.
No test of plateau or of the causes of alignment. Only a brief argument that ViT-Base (from CLIP) also aligns with non-CLIP image models, so the fastText alignment is not merely from CLIP.

missing.what: Per-axis Pearson correlations between matched English and each other-language axis, ICA vs PCA. These show how many axes align and how quickly correlation decays along the axis ordering.

Only 276 ICA axes (292 PCA) were common across all five image models after matching with ViT-Base (768 dims). The authors explicitly name ResMLP and Swin as aligning well with fastText but not ResNet-18, which hints that alignment is weaker for some models.
Language-dependent non-Gaussianity: English is the most spiky and Chinese/Hindi the least (Table 7 skewness/kurtosis). This bears on how uniform the shared structure is.

record.verdict_notes: The reader misassigned columns in Table 3: the two numbers in each supervised row are Original and Random for the same method, not LS and Proc. Correct values: 157langs LS 84.72/55.28 and Proc 84.95/18.72; MUSE LS 78.91/51.44 and Proc 78.41/20.19 (Original/Random). ICA is invariant to invertible linear transforms up to permutation, which explains why its Original and Random scores are nearly equal. MUSE embeddings are pre-aligned, so MUSE rows do not reflect independent training. PCA comparator rows (R2, R4, R6, R8) show that principal-component bases are not shared, which does not count against V5. The core universality evidence is visual (heatmaps), with no reported correlation values.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size or capability sweep; no test of alignment increasing with scale or performance.
Image embeddings are linked to fastText using ImageNet class-name words, not paired captions; no test of alignment increasing as vision and language models improve.
No comparison of same-architecture models trained from different initializations or a test of shared seed-level features/subspaces.

Tests axis alignment by permutation and cross-lingual retrieval, but not stitching, relative representations, or mapping without paired data. The paper notes translation pairs are needed for its correlation-based axis matching.
Tests recurring interpretable semantic axes in embeddings, not neuron-level or SAE-feature/circuit recurrence.
Uses cross-correlation for alignment and compares ICA with PCA transformations; it does not vary the similarity measure, its settings, or the input distribution to test metric/data dependence.
Does not test whether shared data or objectives cause the observed alignment, nor whether alignment plateaus or remains incomplete in representation space.

relationships.condition: ICA axes across 7 languages' fastText, fastText vs BERT, and ViT-Base vs ResMLP-12 / five image models
relationships.reason: The figures show strong diagonal cross-correlations with near-zero off-diagonals, and shared semantic axes such as first names, ships-and-sea and alcohol (R1, R3, R5, R7). The evidence is figure-only and qualitative, with no numeric correlations in the text.
relationships.display_finding: Matched axes showed strong diagonal cross-correlations and near-zero off-diagonals, with shared meanings including first names, ships and sea, and alcohol.

source_check.reason: R1, R3, R5, and R7 document aligned interpretable ICA axes and corresponding semantic patterns across these settings. The evidence concerns extracted feature axes, rather than recurring individual neurons or circuits.

relationships.condition: Supervised linear least-squares map between independently trained 157langs fastText languages
relationships.reason: The LS map reaches 84.72 average top-1 translation retrieval EN→ES/FR/DE/IT/RU (R10). Even under random linear distortion it reaches 55.28 (R14).
relationships.display_finding: Least-squares mapping achieved average top-1 translation retrieval of 84.72 across English-to-Spanish/French/German/Italian/Russian pairs and 55.28 under random linear distortion.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Supervised linear least-squares map between independently trained 157langs fastText languages
source_check.reason: R10 gives 84.72 average held-out translation top-1 accuracy using a simple supervised linear map. Corrected R14 gives 55.28 under random distortion, showing weaker recovery in that condition.

relationships.condition: Permutation-only map between separately ICA-transformed 157langs embeddings
relationships.reason: Matching axes by permutation recovers only 19.48 (Original) and 18.60 (Random) top-1, against LS 84.72 (R9, R13). The shared axes are far from a lossless map, and matching requires paired translation data.
relationships.display_finding: Permutation matching achieved top-1 scores of 19.48 for Original and 18.60 for Random versus least-squares 84.72, while still requiring paired translation data.

relation.reason: The study reports its own comparisons of independently trained embeddings across languages, algorithms, and modalities.

tranche.reason: Separate ICA transformations, matched-axis correlations, semantic heatmaps, and translation retrieval directly test shared features and mappability using a different method.

source_check.notes: ICA fitting is unsupervised, but axis permutation uses paired data and is explicitly supervised in Appendix E.5. Qualitative axis alignment alone does not establish low-loss interchangeability; the authors' broad comparability claim exceeds the 157langs retrieval results.
